transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-10 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62m
Attendees: Maya Cohen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Park (Redwood Infra), Lena Ortiz (Verdant CTO), Markus Engel (Verdant ML), Priya Shah (Verdant Infra), Tom Nguyen (Verdant PM)
Links shared: https://redwood.ai/decks/verdant-rerank-bench.pdf , benchmark spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/verdant-6-10.csv

[00:00] Maya: alright thanks everyone for joining, quick intro; this is the rerank performance + cost deep dive for Verdant, we'll try to focus on the middle mile, cost per query and tail latency at 95/99.
[00:18] Lena: thanks, we have fairly strict SLOs for patient-facing queries, target p95 end-to-end rerank latency is 200ms, ideally 120ms. Right now our candidate generation is ~40ms but rerank is the problem.
[00:36] Ravi: got it, and what volume are we seeing? batch vs single?
[00:44] Markus: baseline is 400 qps peak, but spiky.. burst to 900 qps during morning sync windows, most queries are short, average doc set 120 candidates, we run a dual-stage: embeddings candidate filter then neural reranker.
[01:05] Maya: cool, so main levers we'll discuss: vector dims (we heard you testing 512), batch sizes and continuous vs micro-batching, KV cache for prefix state for long queries, and quantization of embeddings to reduce memory and bandwidth.
[01:25] Tom: also we need to keep data in our VPC, and KMS must be our HSM-backed KMS; on-prem isn't fully air-gapped but that's our constraint.
[01:40] Ravi: okay first, vector dimensionality. there's a linear tradeoff: 512 dims gives slightly better rerank AUC vs 256 but costs ~2x memory and ~1.7x compute for dense matmuls. for Verdant's dataset we saw diminishing returns past 256 for passage-level rerank.
[02:05] Markus: hmm we did a small eval and 128->256 had biggest jump, 256->512 was marginal. but we worry about recall on rare clinical terms.
[02:20] Ravi: right, suggestion: run a targeted eval for rare-term recall as a gated quality check; if it fails, option B is ensemble: 256 embeddings + lexical signals.
[02:36] Jules: on infra side, higher dims mean embedding store memory increases; with shard count 8 per node, 512 dims pushes us to bigger instances or more nodes which means higher network egress within VPC.
[02:56] Lena: can Redwood's runtime do KV caching for rerank? we previously heard KV cache is only for autoregressive generation.
[03:08] Ravi: yeah fair question, our KV cache in the runtime is generic but the big win for rerank is prefix caching of dense candidates and partial dot-product results; we can cache top-k candidate vectors per user session as a warmed prefix to avoid recomputing embeddings for repeated queries. it's called prefix/KV style but in search it's really an item-cache.
[03:35] Markus: are eviction policies LRU? how does it behave under burst loads?
[03:42] Jules: eviction is LRU by default, and we have async background compaction to reduce fragmentation; under bursty load you need to tune cache size and pre-warm strategy, otherwise cold misses will hit quantized fetch and cause tail spikes.
[04:00] Ravi: this relates to batching. continuous batching (streaming into CPU/GPU with very small micro-batches) keeps tail lower for single-req latency compared to large synchronous batches which maximize throughput but increase p95. micro-batches of 8-16 gave best tradeoffs in our internal tests for rerank with 256 dims.
[04:28] Lena: what's the bandwidth penalty when using int8 quantization for embeddings?
[04:34] Ravi: int8 roughly reduces memory/bandwidth 4x vs fp32 and 2x vs fp16; but quality/recall dips depend on embedding model and quant scheme. for our 256-d models we saw 0.8-1.5% drop in rerank AUC using dynamic range int8; productively acceptable if you tune your re-scaling per-shard.
[04:58] Markus: any gotchas with quantization on GPU vs CPU?
[05:03] Jules: fp16 is GPU friendly and most GPUs have native fp16 kernels; int8 often needs specialized kernels or runtime quant path, otherwise CPU dequant is a hotspot. Redwood's runtime uses int8 kernels when available and falls back to fp16-friendly kernels. on-prem hardware variability matters - check kernel support.
[05:30] Tom: network encryption and KMS: when embeddings are served from a private store in our VPC, we need TLS in transit and customer-managed KMS for key wrapping per the compliance doc. is that supported?
[05:44] Maya: yes, Redwood Private supports customer KMS and TLS; for on-prem we need a network diagram and we'll share an ops checklist. Jules, you'll own the infra checklist with Priya.
[05:54] Priya: we'll need mapping of ports and egress expectations; e.g., shard-to-shard traffic during shuffles. can we estimate inter-node traffic for a rerank workload?
[06:06] Ravi: rough rule: for dense rerank, if embedding dims D and shard count S, cross-node traffic per request ~ candidates_per_req * D * sizeof(dtype) / S, plus RPC overhead. so for 120 candidates, D=256, int8 dtype (~1 byte), S=8 -> ~3.8KB per request of raw vector bytes plus headers. but multiply by qps and hot candidate replication, it grows quickly.
[06:34] Markus: that helps; at 900 qps bursts it's non-trivial, we need to size NICs and ensure no egress cost surprise inside cloud.
[06:45] Ravi: also caching hot candidates reduces inter-node reads dramatically. prefetch + warm cache for top-1k items can cut traffic 60-80% for common queries.
[06:58] Lena: what about batch sizes for GPU rendezvous? we have mixed CPU-only and GPU nodes.
[07:05] Jules: for GPU runner, optimal batch size depends on kernel and sequence length — for embeddings matmul it's about maximizing GEMM throughput; for 256 dims we saw best GPU throughput at batch 64-128, but that would violate your p95 SLO. micro-batching lets you keep per-request latency down while still aggregating some work. Redwood supports batching windows with max latency thresholds so you can say: batch up to 50ms or 32 requests, whichever first.
[07:36] Tom: can we do hybrid: CPU-run small batches and spill to GPU for heavy batched jobs?
[07:42] Ravi: yes, routing policies can send latency-sensitive requests to CPU-serving replicas with lightweight models and route bulk/background rerank to GPU pools. this is where cost controls come in.
[07:56] Markus: curious about cost math: for 256 dims with int8 on GPU and batching, what's token or QPU equivalent?
[08:06] Maya: we provide per-request cost estimates in spreadsheet; quick ballpark: for dense matmul heavy rerank, cost is dominated by compute and memory bandwidth; moving from 512->256 dims roughly halves compute and memory cost. choosing int8 vs fp16 halves memory cost but may require specialized nodes. We'll send conservative numbers in benchmark sheet.
[08:30] Lena: tails — we care about p99 more than average. what strategies reduce p99?
[08:37] Ravi: strategies: pre-warming hot candidate cache, throttling bursts with circuit breakers, hybrid routing to redundant replicas, and slack heterogenous batching windows (small max latency window). also enable early-exit reranker (cheap model to filter) to avoid full NN rerank on many queries.
[08:56] Markus: early-exit sounds interesting. do you have an example?
[09:00] Ravi: e.g., a logistic regression on BM25+light embedding dot gives >80% filter and only passes top ~30 to NN reranker. reduces avg compute dramatically.
[09:12] Priya: for on-prem, we need to understand data residency and audit logs - does Redwood Private produce request-level audit logs with masked PII?
[09:23] Maya: yes, Private provides audit trails, request hashing and optional redaction. logs can be pushed to customer's SIEM via syslog or S3. we'll attach the security datasheet.
[09:34] Tom: ok next, benchmarking plan and success criteria?
[09:38] Ravi: propose three bench configs: A) 256 dims fp16, micro-batch 8, hot cache pre-warm 1k items; B) 256 dims int8, micro-batch 16, pre-warm 500; C) 128 dims fp16 with lexical ensemble; measure p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, AUC on golden set, and network egress. run each under steady 400 qps and burst 900 qps for 10m windows.
[10:10] Markus: acceptable thresholds: p95 < 200ms, p99 < 500ms, AUC drop < 1.5% vs current. If config B meets those, we prefer B for cost.
[10:24] Maya: we'll instrument to produce per-route token/cost and include cost per million queries estimate.
[10:31] Lena: timeline?
[10:34] Maya: Redwood team can deliver bench configs and run managed benchmark in our hosted sandbox or provide helm charts for private run. preferred: run in Verdant private VPC to capture network behavior. schedule the run week of 6/22.
[10:48] Tom: ok any competitors or alternatives under consideration?
[10:51] Lena: VectorCloud and a self-build route are both floated, VectorCloud pitched cheaper but had less robust KV cache.
[10:58] Ravi: we'll highlight differences in the follow-up doc.
[11:03] Maya: quick recap before we wrap: Redwood to share benchmark configs and spreadsheet (Ravi), Verdant to send sample queries + labels (Markus), infra checklist (Jules + Priya) for VPC/KMS, and schedule the private bench run week of 6/22.
[11:18] Priya: noted. also will follow up on allowed ports and egress cost concerns.
[11:24] Lena: thanks all, this was helpful.
[11:28] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll send the summary and action items.
[11:33] END TRANSCRIPT
